newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African soldiers militate for trade union rights.
newsitem.headline: S.African soldiers militate for trade union rights.

text.p: South African soldiers allied to a fledgling trade union on Wednesday accused the national defence force of infringing their constitutional rights by barring free labour practise.
The South African National Defence Union said in a statement it was considering High Court action to secure troops the right to freedom of expression and permission to join a union.
The union charged that senior army officers had tried to force troops to sign a document waiving their constitutional rights, barring them from wearing union T-shirts or organising for the union.

Calling for the document to be withdrawn, the union said: "SANDU is at present consulting with our legal representatives for advice on the possibility of these special orders constituting an urgent basis for an High Court application."
Army spokeswoman Major Merle Meyer, while confirming troops were not permitted to join a union, denied soldiers has been asked to sign the document.

"Soldiers are told in information bulletins, which are open (to the media and public scrutiny), advising them that they may not join a union but there is not a document they have to sign," she told Reuters.
Meyer said the army did not recognise the union as the military was classified as an essential service which forbids soldiers from embarking on strike action.
"But it's not as if the soldiers have been left in the lurch. There are various channels where soldiers can address their grievances," she added.

South Africa has adopted labour-friendly laws and integrated its military across the race divide since the black-led African National Congress (ANC) won power in 1994, but has not relaxed legislation governing the military.
